prompt.en: A whole-cable ferrite reduces RF that flows the same way on both power leads, but a different noise current flowing out on one lead and back on the other remains. Why?

text.en: The remaining noise is probably generated inside the receiver, since the cable cure has already been applied.

feedback.en: An external noise current can remain when the cure does not address its path. One cable test does not locate the remaining source.

text.en: The ferrite is probably damaged, since success on one cable current should carry over to the other.

feedback.en: The two current paths interact differently with a whole-cable core. Different results do not by themselves indicate damage.

text.en: The first current was common mode; the second is differential mode and may need a different filter.

feedback.en: A whole-cable choke mainly impedes common-mode RF. It is not a universal cure for differential noise.

text.en: A ferrite should mainly block the intended DC current, so both tests used the wrong principle.

feedback.en: The intended out-and-back current is usually left mostly unchanged; unwanted common-mode current is the target.

explanation.en: Identify how the unwanted current travels before expecting the same cure to work on every noise path.

prompt.en: A noise test combines switching off a charger with rerouting the receiver cable. The noise falls. Which follow-up would best identify which change helped?

text.en: Test the two changes separately with brief, repeatable comparisons.

feedback.en: Changing one thing at a time separates their effects. The combined result does not tell whether the charger change, cable route, or both mattered.

text.en: Attribute the improvement to the charger because powered devices are more likely sources than cables.

feedback.en: That is a hypothesis, not a result of this test. The cable change may have reduced pickup even if the charger was involved.

text.en: Attribute the improvement to the cable because it is closer to the receiver.

feedback.en: Physical closeness alone does not isolate the cause. The charger was also changed, so its contribution remains unresolved.

text.en: Leave the charger off and compare noise at two nearby receive frequencies on the new cable route.

feedback.en: Changing receive frequency can characterize the noise, but both original changes remain applied. It does not separate the charger contribution from the cable-route effect.

explanation.en: A combined test can show improvement without identifying its cause. Separate the changes before choosing which cure to keep.

prompt.en: A filter rejects the unwanted frequency correctly, but it was designed for a different nominal impedance than the receiver line. Why can wanted-signal delivery still suffer?

text.en: The measured rejection is enough to approve the filter without a wanted-band check.

feedback.en: Good rejection at the unwanted frequency does not establish acceptable wanted-band transfer in the installed system.

text.en: An impedance mismatch can cause reflections and loss even when the rejected frequency is right.

feedback.en: Match the filter to the line and equipment as well as choosing the correct response.

text.en: The rejection measurement is evidence that the cable has taken on the filter's nominal impedance.

feedback.en: The cable keeps the characteristic impedance set by its own construction. One rejection measurement does not establish the system match.

text.en: A better station-end reading after adding coax is enough evidence to keep the filter.

feedback.en: A changed line length can improve a reading through impedance transformation. It does not establish that the filter transfers the wanted signal well in this system.

explanation.en: Frequency selection, impedance, and placement are separate filter requirements.
